summary: This document specifies how the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) protocol is used on IPFIX Mediators, which are devices that sit between collectors and exporters of network traffic data. It covers Template and Observation Point management, timing considerations, and other concerns specific to Mediators.

eli5.summary: Think of a helper who stands between people counting cars on a road and the office that wants the totals. This document explains how that helper should pass the counts along properly.

questions: what is a template mapping in ipfix
subtitle: How the IPFIX flow-export protocol must behave when a device in the middle re-exports flow data.

tldr.problem: IPFIX was not originally written with Mediators in mind, devices that collect flow records and export them again. Template IDs, Observation Domain IDs, timestamps and the identity of the original exporter can all be lost or clash.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds rules for Template Mapping, Observation Domain ID handling, timestamps, transport and unknown Information Elements. It also defines five new Information Elements for original exporter, original domain and Intermediate Process statistics.
tldr.outcome: All Intermediate Processes must comply with these rules, with extra rules per process type living in their own documents. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7119 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the document that defines how IPFIX behaves on Mediators, building on RFC 7011.

sections.title: Why Mediators Need Their Own Rules
sections.content:
The IPFIX protocol (RFC 7011) exports information about IP traffic Flows from an Exporter to a Collector. It was not originally written with IPFIX Mediators in mind. A Mediator is a device that contains both a Collecting Process and an Exporting Process, so it receives a record stream, transforms it with one or more Intermediate Processes, and exports the result.

Putting IPFIX inside a Mediator affects the technical details. The problem statement (RFC 5982) lists the issues: loss of original Exporter information, loss of base time information, transport session management, loss of Options Template information, Template ID management, network topology, interpretation and aggregation. This RFC builds on RFC 7011 and the Mediation Framework (RFC 6183). All of RFC 7011 applies unless this document says otherwise.

Because the PSAMP protocol (RFC 5476) is based on IPFIX, the same rules also apply to PSAMP.
sections.eli5: A normal counter reports straight to the office. A helper in the middle changes the story a little, so the helper needs extra rules to keep the facts straight.

sections.title: Message Headers from a Mediator
sections.content:
The IPFIX Message Header a Mediator sends is identical to the one in RFC 7011, with the fields Version, Length, Export Time, Sequence Number and Observation Domain ID. Export Time and Observation Domain ID can be handled differently at a Mediator.

Export Time is the time the message leaves the Mediator. A Mediator that contains an Intermediate Conversion Process MAY instead reuse the export time received on the incoming Transport Session.

Observation Domain ID is a 32-bit identifier. It is set to 0 when no specific domain is relevant for the whole message, for example when aggregated Data Records are exported to a hierarchy of Collectors.

If a Mediator receives messages made of Template Withdrawals and Template Sets and forwards them, it MUST NOT change the Set order or the message order.
sections.eli5: Every parcel has a label. The helper stamps the label with the time it sends the parcel on, and uses a zero for the label when a parcel mixes things from several places.

sections.title: Template Management and the Template Mapping
sections.content:
Template IDs are unique per Exporter, per Transport Session and per Observation Domain. Nothing guarantees that the ID used on the incoming session matches the one used on the outgoing session. How a Mediator copes depends on its Intermediate Process, and there are two cases.

Unmodified Templates (Section 4.1). A Mediator that passes substantially the same Data Records downstream, such as an Intermediate Flow Selection Process that redirects records to different Collectors, MUST keep a Template Mapping. It links each received (Options) Template Record to each exported one, along with Template ID, Observation Domain ID, Transport Session information and metadata scoped to the Template, such as the flowKeyIndicator.

  • If a received Template is withdrawn and no other mapping uses it, the Mediator SHOULD export a withdrawal on the outgoing session and remove the entry.
  • A Template no longer used on an outgoing session MUST be withdrawn there and its entry removed.
  • When a Transport Session is gracefully shut down or reset, its Template entries MUST be removed.

New Templates (Section 4.2). A Mediator whose output is substantially changed generates its own Templates and needs no mapping. Some cases still keep one, for example an anonymization process that must remember which derived Template came from which received one.

Ordering: Template Records with identical Information Elements in a different order SHOULD be treated as identical. Options Templates whose Scope fields have the same elements in a different order MUST be treated as semantically different.
sections.eli5: The helper keeps a notebook that says 'what the counter called box 258, I call box 256 when I send it to the north office'. Without the notebook, the offices would open the wrong boxes.

sections.title: Original Exporter, Observation Domain and Unknown Elements
sections.content:
Unknown Information Elements (Section 4.3). A Mediator that does not generate new Records SHOULD re-export values for Information Elements it does not understand, and MUST NOT omit or reorder fields in such records. A Mediator that does generate new Records MUST ignore values it does not understand. Either way it SHOULD log the fact.

Original Observation Point (Section 5). Without extra information, a Collector may wrongly conclude that the Mediator itself saw the packets. Two new Information Elements, originalExporterIPv4Address (ElementId 403) and originalExporterIPv6Address (ElementId 404), carry the address of the Original Exporter as seen by the Mediator. A Mediator MAY export richer Observation Point descriptions, in which case it MUST use the structured data of RFC 6313, for instance a subTemplateMultiList with the semantic exactlyOneOf. A Mediator SHOULD NOT replace a received original address with its own, with known exceptions such as anonymization and NAT address rewriting.

Observation Domain IDs (Section 6). A Mediator that does not change Templates MUST use a Template Mapping so that Observation Domain ID and Template ID combinations do not collide. One that creates new Templates can either give itself its own independent Observation Domains or keep a mapping. When the header cannot hold a consistent domain, the new originalObservationDomainId (ElementId 405) carries the original value, and a Mediator MUST NOT modify it.
sections.eli5: When the helper passes counts on, it writes 'originally counted by Road Crew 7' next to them, so the office does not think the helper stood at the roadside.

sections.title: Timing, Transport and Reporting
sections.content:
Timing (Section 7). Mediators are RECOMMENDED to use absolute timestamps such as flowStartSeconds, flowStartMilliseconds or flowStartNanoseconds, rather than relative ones such as flowStartSysUpTime or flowStartDeltaMicroseconds. Relative values need constant translation, and with the delta-microsecond elements a Data Record must be exported within a maximum of 71 minutes because the 32-bit counter would otherwise overflow.

Intermediate Processes MUST NOT assume that records arrive ordered by flowStartTime, flowEndTime or observationTime. They MAY ignore records significantly out of order, but SHOULD report that records were dropped. When aggregating, exported timestamps SHOULD be the minimum of the start times and the maximum of the end times.

Transport (Section 8). SCTP with the PR-SCTP extension MUST be implemented by all compliant Mediators. TCP and UDP MAY also be implemented. SCTP SHOULD be used where links may be congested. UDP is not congestion-aware, so IPFIX traffic over UDP MUST run in an environment where it has been provisioned for or separated from other traffic.

Reporting (Section 10). Mediators MAY implement an Intermediate Process Reliability Statistics Options Template. It uses two new elements, intermediateProcessId (ElementId 406) and ignoredDataRecordTotalCount (ElementId 407). If a Mediator exports different Flow Keys from those it received and the Original Exporter sent a Flow Keys Options record, the Mediator MUST export a new Flow Keys Options record.
sections.eli5: Use a wall clock time rather than 'ten minutes ago', because 'ten minutes ago' stops making sense once the message has been passed along. And tell the office how many counts you had to skip.

sections.title: Security and Operations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7011 apply to Mediators, and so do those for IPFIX Files (RFC 5655) if the Mediator writes or stores files. The RFC is blunt that Mediators are by design "men in the middle". A Mediator can use the exporterCertificate and collectorCertificate elements to report X.509 identities of upstream TLS sessions, but this cannot give true end-to-end assurance, because any Mediator in a chain can falsify what it reports. Information about the chain of mediation must be determined out of band.

An Exporting Process has no in-band way to tell whether a Collecting Process will act as a Mediator. Trust placed in Collecting Processes is absolute, so care is needed when exporting between parties controlled by different entities.

Operationally, combining data from several Original Exporters requires consistently configured Metering Processes. Consistency should be verified out of band, for example with the MIB modules (RFC 6615, RFC 6727) or the configuration data model (RFC 6728). Careless configuration can lead to collected data being misinterpreted.
sections.eli5: The helper sits in the middle, so the office has to trust the helper completely. The helper could say anything, so who you let be the helper matters.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: IPFIX version; 0x000a for the current version.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length of the message in octets, including header and Sets.

fields.name: Export Time
fields.desc: Seconds since the UNIX epoch when the message leaves the Mediator.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Counter modulo 2^32 of Data Records sent in the stream.

fields.name: Observation Domain ID
fields.desc: Identifies the Observation Domain; 0 when none is relevant.
